newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila defence chief declares presidential bid.
newsitem.headline: Manila defence chief declares presidential bid.

text.p: Philippine Defence Secretary Renato de Villa on Saturday declared himself a candidate in the 1998 elections to choose the successor to President Fidel Ramos.
De Villa, 61, said he would seek the nomination of Ramos' Lakas (People's Power) party to be its standard bearer in the presidential contest scheduled for May next year.

"Considering the public record behind me (and) that I would be able to do more for our people as their leader...I decided to offer myself (as candidate)," de Villa told a news conference. The former general joins about a dozen other politicians who have expressed interest in succeeding Ramos, who is barred from running for a second term under the constitution, which limits a president to one six- year term.
Ramos has repeatedly said he will step down when his term ends in June 1998 and has denied he is behind moves by a citizens group to amend the constitution to allow him to run for another term.
De Villa said he would run only under the Lakas party and would not seek any other party's nomination if he failed to get its support.
The party has yet to decide when it will meet to consider who will be its standard bearer.

Vice President Joseph Estrada, who belongs to the opposition Nationalist Peoples Coalition, and opposition Senator Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, have consistently topped most poll surveys on who Filipinos favoured as their presidential candidate. Although de Villa rated low in most surveys, he emerged as the business community's top choice in a poll conducted by the Makati Business Club in February.

Others who have expressed interest in succeeding Ramos are his sister and senator Leticia Ramos Shahani, Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo, House of Representatives Speaker Jose de Venecia and several other senators.
De Villa has been described by Manila's media as a Ramos "clone" because of supposed similarities in their leadership style and coincidental patterns in their careers.
When he took over the post of national police chief in 1986, he was stepping into the slot vacated by Ramos, who had been promoted then to armed forces chief of staff.
When Ramos moved on to become defence secretary, it was de Villa who succeeded him as military chief.
Together, they led loyalist forces in crushing six army coup attempts against then president Corazon Aquino.
When Ramos gave up the defence post to run for president in 1992, Aquino picked de Villa as new defence secretary.
